The word heading has several distinct meanings depending on the context. All of them share a common thread: something that tops, leads, or points forward. Here is every important meaning explained fully.
1. A title or label at the top of written content

This is the most common meaning in everyday life. A heading is a short piece of text placed at the top of a page, section, chapter, document, email, or any block of content. Its purpose is to tell you — before you read — what the content below is about. Think of it as a signpost.

A heading is always meant to be brief and informative. It prepares the reader for what follows.

Examples:

  • A newspaper article has a heading (the bold line at the top — what people commonly call a headline) that tells you what the story is about.
  • A book chapter might have the heading "Chapter 4: The Journey Begins."
  • A long report might have multiple headings like "Introduction," "Findings," and "Conclusion" to divide it into clear sections.
  • A form might have headings like "Personal Details" or "Payment Information" to group related fields together.
  • An official letter often begins with a heading that states the sender's address and the date.

When a document has smaller titles beneath the main heading, those are called subheadings. For example, a chapter called "Health" might have subheadings like "Diet," "Exercise," and "Sleep" within it. Subheadings break a large section into smaller, more navigable parts.

In digital writing — word processors like Microsoft Word, Google Docs, or web pages — headings are a formal structural feature. In HTML (the language of websites), headings are tagged as H1, H2, H3, and so on, where H1 is the most important (usually the page title), H2 is a section title, H3 is a subsection title, and so forth. This hierarchy helps both readers and search engines understand the structure of the content.

In a legal or official document, the heading of a section is the short descriptive label that identifies what that section covers. Courts and lawmakers use it to summarize a clause before its full text.

In navigation — whether by sea or air — a heading is the direction a vehicle is pointing, expressed as a compass bearing measured in degrees.

Imagine a full circle with 360 degrees. North is 0° (or 360°), East is 90°, South is 180°, and West is 270°. Every direction between these can be expressed as a number in degrees.

Examples:

  • "The captain ordered a heading of 270 degrees" — meaning the ship is now pointing due west.
  • "Maintain your current heading" — the pilot should keep flying in the same direction.
  • "We changed our heading to avoid the storm."

An important distinction — heading vs. course:
A heading is where the vehicle is pointed. But because of wind (for aircraft) or ocean currents (for ships), the vehicle may not actually travel in the exact direction it is pointing. The actual path the vehicle traces over the ground is called the course (or track). For example, a plane pointed east (heading: 090°) may be drifted slightly southeast by strong crosswinds, so its actual course over the ground is 110°. Pilots and navigators must account for this difference.

In casual, everyday language, people also use "heading" loosely to mean general direction — "We were on a heading toward the mountains" — even when no precise degrees are involved.
3. A tunnel driven into rock (mining and civil engineering)

In mining and tunneling, a heading is a horizontal tunnel or passage that is dug forward into the rock face or earth.

It is typically a narrow, preliminary tunnel cut into the mine to explore, access, or prepare an area for larger excavation. Miners drive a heading — meaning they progressively dig it forward, advancing its length over time.

Examples:

  • "The miners advanced the heading by fifteen meters this week."
  • "A new heading was opened to reach the coal seam."
  • "The heading collapsed before they could shore it up."

The word is used this way because the tunnel is literally "heading into" the rock — pushing forward into uncharted material.
4. The top section of a curtain (interior design and soft furnishing)

In curtain-making and home furnishing, the heading is the top part of a curtain — the section at the very top where the fabric is gathered, folded, or pleated so it can be attached to a curtain rod, track, or rail.

The heading determines both the visual style of the curtain (how it hangs and drapes) and how much fabric is needed to make it. Different heading styles are named and widely recognized in this field:

  • Pencil pleat heading — The fabric at the top is gathered into tight, narrow, cylindrical pleats that look like a row of pencils standing side by side. This is the most traditional style.
  • Eyelet heading — Large metal rings (eyelets) are punched through the top of the fabric at regular intervals, and the curtain rod passes directly through these rings. This gives a modern, casual look.
  • Tab top heading — Loops of fabric (tabs) are sewn at the top, and the rod threads through them.
  • Pinch pleat heading — The fabric is pinched into deep, formal pleats at regular intervals and stitched in place. This is a classic, tailored look.
  • Wave heading — The fabric flows in soft, even, uniform waves. Often used in contemporary interiors.

Examples:

  • "She chose an eyelet heading for the bedroom curtains because it looked more relaxed."
  • "The heading needs to be at least 15 cm deep for the pleats to form properly."
  • "When buying fabric for curtains with a pencil pleat heading, you typically need two to two-and-a-half times the width of the window."
5. The act of hitting a ball with the head (football/soccer) — less common

In British English, particularly in football (soccer), a heading can refer to the act of deliberately striking the ball with one's head to pass it, control it, or score. However, this usage is less common as a noun — the word header is far more frequently used in this sense today.

  • More common: "He scored with a brilliant header."
  • Less common but valid: "His heading of the ball into the net was perfectly timed."

You might encounter this in older writing or formal match reports.

Every sense of the word "heading" shares an underlying idea: something that is at the top, at the front, or points forward.

  • A document heading sits at the top of the content.
  • A navigation heading points the vehicle forward in a direction.
  • A mining heading pushes forward into rock.
  • A curtain heading is at the top of the curtain.
  • A football heading uses the top of the body (the head) to play the ball.

Once you see this, the word becomes easy to understand in any context — whatever is leading or topping something is its heading.
